7.t: Snooky's, Morris Levy and Dizzy's house loan
7.s: Thomas books Dizzy at Snooky's when Levy won't pay more, then gets Levy to lend six thousand dollars and raise him to fifteen hundred.
7.q: Yeah. Dizzy was a good comedian, so... I got involved with that a little bit when Snooky was on 45th Street or 44th Street, and that's how I got close to Dizzy. Because I got him the job down there... Because I was having trouble with Morris Levy. Morris Levy didn't want to pay him more... We was…

7.t: Booking Bill Davis and Billy Shaw's commission
7.s: Thomas begins booking organist Bill Davis, and works with Billy Shaw on a five percent commission.
7.q: I was just a part of it then. And Snooky's just kind of gave me my start. Because I found out I could book. Then I signed up... Then I went down to Atlantic City, and I heard Bill Davis, and that sucker was playing so much organ on that organ... So I asked him, I said, "Man, I'd like to book you."…

7.t: Touring with Bill Davis and running his own booking office
7.s: He manages Bill Davis in California for a hundred dollars and expenses and back home runs his own saxophone-studio booking office.
7.q: So when another guy quit at Shaw, he came... I had gone to California with Bill Davis. Because I worked out a deal with him. I was only making about fifty dollars commission. So I worked out a deal with him if he could give me another fifty dollars, making my salary a hundred dollars and my…

7.t: Joining Billy Shaw's agency; Bill Davis at Birdland; Joe Glaser
7.s: Shaw persuades him to become an agent; he gets Bill Davis into Birdland and recalls Joe Glaser wanting big records.
7.q: Yeah, right. So Billy Shaw called me over. He'd lost a guy, and he wanted to hire me as an agent. And I wasn't too cool about being an agent, but I was really disgusted with my operation going on, because they just wasn't takin' care of business back here like I wanted it to be taken care of.…

7.t: Booking for Shaw: what Calloway taught him
7.s: He explains why booking appealed, how Cab's work taught him to book, and that Bill Davis wouldn't listen when getting twenty-five hundred dollars.
7.q: And you know, all the time I was looking at teaching. That's why I studied with Timothy. His office was next door to me. I used to go in and get my books and practice in his office. And man, I'm so grateful to that man.

7.t: Booking Ray Charles on his first concert
7.s: Seeing Ray Charles play dances to poorly dressed crowds, Thomas books him on concerts and proposes a double of Newark and Carnegie Hall.
7.q: Yeah. I'm the first one to book Ray Charles on a concert. Because I used to go to all his dances to hear what he was doing. You know? Because the guy had such good records, and I wanted to see how he was performing. He always had a good band. But I just noticed in all the places I went, I never…

7.t: Carnegie Hall double, Dinah Washington and Ray Charles as concert artist
7.s: Ray Charles accepts a thousand dollars for both dates, Thomas adds Dinah Washington, and Thursday at Connors Beach proves his concert appeal.
7.q: And he took the double date for the second... He didn't ask for no more... I was giving him a thousand dollars a date. He didn't ask for another penny to double from Newark to Carnegie Hall. But I always will believe...

7.t: Booking territories and Thomas's best region
7.s: He explains how agencies divided territories and why his Richmond to Buffalo territory was the best in the country.
7.q: Yes. That was my territory. And I found out mathematically that I had the best territory in the whole United States. Because I had the biggest towns within a short...a certain distance... I had (?) Washington and Trenton (I booked the college in Trenton), I had New York, and then I had New Haven, I…

7.t: Billy Shaw on commissions and the union rules
7.s: Shaw's fifteen percent arrangement, union limits on commissions, and the former 350-mile booking rule.
7.q: Billy Shaw. He was to me one of the greatest agents that got in this business. He worked one of the big agencies; I think William Morris or something. But all he knew... He told me one day, he said, 'Walter, 15 percent is a lot of money.' He found out he could make 15 percent on one-nighters. He…

7.t: Taking on Fats Domino and booking two weeks of dates
7.s: Given Domino in January, Thomas books him for two-week runs of Mondays through Thursdays in short jumps.
7.q: Oh, it was the late Fifties or early Sixties. I had heard about him, but I didn't know how good he was. I got so mad that I didn't send out nobody. Because here I got this big artist, and they tell me he's good, he's doing so much business. So I got the idea to hear that ...(?)... I had been…

7.t: Persuading Domino to play Las Vegas
7.s: Domino balked at six thousand dollars, but Thomas told him Vegas would set him for life; his gambling debt is mentioned.
7.q: Well, the guy that bought the company, I think he made a deal with Joe Glaser to pick him up. And now Joe Glaser's office books him.

7.t: Rivalry with Dick Boom over booking
7.s: A competing agent resented Thomas for tying up territory, refused to book with him, then joined his office.
7.q: Well, he didn't like me... He didn't like me, because if he had an attraction to book in this territory, my territory, he couldn't get through. Because see, I booked...

7.t: B.B. King, Queen Booking and Ruth Bowen
7.s: Thomas regrets missing B.B. King and describes Ruth Bowen, his saxophone-studio tenant, becoming Dinah Washington's manager.
7.q: Yeah. The one guy I missed on was B.B. King. If I'd had the knowledge that I know now... See, I went to work for Queen, which wasn't aware of the booking business like Shaw was. And I...

7.t: Ruth Bowen's license, gangsters and missing contracts
7.s: Thomas explains how Joe Glaser helped Bowen get licensed, and her mistakes with gangsters and no contracts.
7.q: Yeah. So she got involved in starting an agency. And Joe Glaser was instrumental in getting her the license. Because all she had to do was...

7.t: Advice on starting in personal management; why he has no license
7.s: Thomas advises getting the right agent, explains why he never took an agency license, and Bill Doggett and Bill Davis leaving him.
7.q: Well, I found out in my situation, I used to think that I was a musician and I could book. Any musician can book himself anywhere.

7.t: Lessons from Calloway; Dizzy, Joe Carroll and Moody
7.s: He says Cab's band taught him booking and publicity, regrets losing Dizzy, and mentions Joe Carroll and James Moody.
7.q: Well, I'll tell you. I learned so much about the booking business and the personal management business just being with Calloway. By me being close to him, I saw all the things that Mills did, and the decisions that Cab made. And I learned that. Because I found out one thing about an artist. The one…

7.t: Why Black agencies failed: Ray Charles, Joe Adams and John Lee
7.s: Thomas says Ray Charles now books himself, explains how his agency's new owner botched a complaint, and mentions John Lee managing Nancy Wilson.
7.q: Yeah, because Ray Charles books himself now. He's got a guy that works for him, and he books himself. He's got big enough to do that.

7.t: Driving to Boston to hear Domino
7.s: Puzzled by how easy he was to book, Thomas drives to Boston, finds a New Orleans band and screaming fans, and predicts Domino will be as big as Fats Waller.
7.q: And I said to myself... I booked him for the first week so fast, I said, "Let me go up to Boston and hear this son-of-a-gun, because something's wrong. I ain't never had nobody that easy to book." He was only making $350 or $400 a night. So I...

7.t: Ray Charles the jazz artist; a flop Philadelphia date
7.s: Thomas learns Ray Charles had played with Lowell Fulsom and was really a jazz artist, and misbooks New York musicians for his first Philadelphia date.
7.q: Because I didn't know when I first got involved with Ray Charles that he was a Jazz artist. I just didn't know that. He was singing Rock-and-Roll! And I talked to him one day, and he said, "Well, you know, Walter, I started recording Rock-and-Roll to make money." He knew he was a Jazz artist, but…

7.t: R&B audiences wanted singing, not jazz
7.s: At a Wilmington dance the crowd waited outside for Ray Charles, so Thomas tells him his band must play R&B.
7.q: He used to play dances... I was down at a dance in Wilmington, Delaware, he was playing... And the band used to play an hour before he came on. And the guys was playin', and nobody was going in the hall! All the people were standing outside waiting. So I just looked at it, and I said to myself...…

7.t: Starting personal management with Dizzy Gillespie
7.s: Teaching led to managing; Dizzy gave him a year, and Thomas advised Dizzy to go to England first as a single.
7.q: Yeah. Let me tell you how that happened. See, by being involved in the teaching, I got involved with personal management. I remember one of the first groups I got was Bill Davis. I used to go down to Atlantic City... And one of the first guys that I had a personal management on was Dizzy. You know,…

232.t: Booking agencies after Alexander, and Helen Humes
232.s: Fields lists the agencies that booked him, including Joe Artis and the Ferguson Brothers, and a tour with Helen Humes.
232.q: Numerous others, I'd say, to tell you the truth, ten. Maybe that's why I didn't get any higher. I did most of it and Joe Artis (phonetic spelling) Corporation

232.t: Dishonest booking practices of the Shaw Agency and Joe Glaser
232.s: He caught the Shaw agency in split commissions and notes how Glaser protected Hampton's interests.
232.q: Oh, sure, you run into that. Now I'll tell you, there was a Shaw Booking Agency, now they had their way of showing you, but I called their hand several times and I found out that was going on, where they get it. In other words what I'm talking about, Walt Foots--Foots left Cab Calloway, he

232.t: The Teaspoon booking: a rock group, bad cars and a small-claims suit
232.s: Fields books a local rock group for a Fort Smith date, the cars break down, the promoter pays little, and the group sues in small-claims court.
232.q: roll bunch, and to show you how just a record can excite somebody sometime, because I thought about what I would have done, like I was telling you about that Frisco--I'll send you some tapes from one little record--but a little group named Teaspoon had made a record, just a little local group in…

232.t: How Harry Burns of New Orleans began booking the band
232.s: In McAlester, Oklahoma, agent Harry Burns, born Bernstein, meets Fields and books three or four dates.
232.q: And then another--as I said perhaps so many in between, almost too numerous to name, but one I will not pass up, was Harry Burns. It was kind of odd and strange the way it came about. I was in McAlester, Oklahoma, which you consider that my territory booking, and Harry Burns then was booking--do…

232.t: The Miami and Fort Lauderdale garnishee over a contract clause
232.s: A hidden clause barred playing Fort Lauderdale near Miami; a deputy tries to tie up his money and bus, but a lawyer says the bus cannot be seized.
232.q: That was before the In The Mood days. That must have been around fifty six or seven; somewhere along in there. We started on this tour and sure enough, we opened in Miami and it was during that area in the south, in Florida, all the

232.t: Burns taking bank deposits for dates Fields did not know about
232.s: Burns collects money from military bases for return dates Fields never contracted, and the FBI moves in.
232.q: So Burns was just doing fine and was tickled and all until Burns went to taking money from those army bases and air force bases, and one thing about it, he never would (inaudible), I wouldn't know anything about the contract, and so a lot of it was return dates the second round, so they had had my…

232.t: The FBI looking for Harry Burns in Vernal, Utah
232.s: Singer Al Harris joins the band in Utah and is grilled by an agent about Burns, whom Fields never finds again.
232.q: We were in Frisco at the time and (inaudible)--we'd been working so steady, a very fine vocalist in the band and he told us that when we get back this time to headquarters--his headquarters was Kansas City--he said I'm going home and stay a while, we've been going at it and I've got to spend a…

232.t: Playing the University of Miami homecoming, a first for a Black band
232.s: Burns persuades Miami students to fly the band in for homecoming; Fields shows a photo with Dr. Thurston Adams.
232.q: We made this round on and on and I will say that I have a write up there that Burns is responsible for and we'll send that in to Ron too, The University of Miami. You see, by Burns booking the Wings over (inaudible), he just knew when they'd be in the south or when they'd be in the north and so he…

232.t: Reg Marshall as booking agent: Los Angeles dates and the 5-4 Ballroom
232.s: Reg Marshall got Fields into the Club Alabam after Kenton, the 5-4 Ballroom and Vancouver; Fields thought him honest because he wasn't big enough to cheat.
232.q: Oh, yes, Reg Marshall booked me quite a bit. I'm glad you thought of that, because I forgot about him. He got me some pretty nice spots, I mentioned I think, about Schoonover, that carried me west, but like sandlot and big league, Reg--

231.t: Nazarro, the William Morris office and breaking away
231.s: On Nazarro's long hold over them, he says William Morris cut the act's price and offered a Chicago contract.
231.q: it, you see, the Jewish people are very clannish, they stick together, you know. If you told a Jewish friend over there how rotten I was, he'd take your word for it, you understand? More so than he would take somebody else's word saying I was good and the other person was a different nationality.…

231.s: Handled by Glaser at Associated Booking, he says the difference from Nazarro was night and day.
231.ch: Solo years, marriages and the Canadian party
231.q: Oh, Lord, the difference was night and day, different as night and day. So much difference, he's a polished man compared to him. You know? He was a pleasure to work for and a pleasure to work with in my book.

231.t: Buck's passive role and Bubbles as a father to him
231.s: Bubbles handled all the business; Buck was satisfied as he was and would have stayed in Kentucky.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: No, he didn't have that kind of mind. He was satisfied as he was. Just like Chuck would be satisfied as he is if nobody enlightened him on anything, he'd be stay put. And that's the same way Buck was. I had to get him out of Kentucky. I had to teach him how to be and act in public. I was just like…

231.t: Nazarro's other acts and playing one performer against another
231.s: Bubbles let Nazarro represent other Negro acts, who then were pushed forward on the strength of the Buck and Bubbles name.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: Oh, many of them. He had a lot. In fact his office was the only office that had more than one negro act, because I'm the one that let them have the other negro acts because I wanted the other negroes to get jobs. But Bill Robinson and Ethel Waters, they were too individual and selfish to allow…

231.t: Why Nazarro favored other acts over Buck and Bubbles
231.s: Nazarro could book weaker acts like Heckle and Jive cheaply and sell them for more, claiming they were as good as Buck and Bubbles.
231.ch: Blackbirds, Carmen Jones and the Ziegfeld Follies
231.q: Oh, man. Listen. He would book them for instance for $100, sell them for $350, understand, or $300, tell them they're a better act than Buck and Bubbles or as good as Buck and Bubbles you just haven't seen them that's all. Just that they've been out.

231.t: How long they had been with Nazarro by 1921
231.s: Pressed on the chronology, Bubbles says they had been together two years, 1919-21, and that Nazarro was selfish and kept them from a name.
231.q: I played the Columbia Theater, I went off to California, I'm just coming to California. How much time have I had to find out? That's the first time I saw two checks for the act of Buck and Bubbles. How could I do that? Go ahead, you tell me. Have you been following the story? You missed it.

231.t: The five-year management contract Buck signed alone
231.s: Nazarro got Buck to sign a five-year contract without Bubbles, who could not go on without his partner.
231.q: Almost the same thing -- five years, five-year agreement. It was five years and I had to take on top of what Buck did. See, I wasn't going to sign no more with him from the time I told you concerning the case. I was just going to just stall around and not play no more. But he got Buck to sign a…

382.t: Columbia's artist bureau, Sonny Werblin and MCA vaudeville dates
382.s: When Columbia gave up its bureau she dealt with Sonny Werblin and MCA, with disappointing theater dates in a few cities.
382.q: I don't know whether I mentioned this before or not, but during the time when I was making my earlier recordings, I was under exclusive contract to Columbia Records.

382.t: The management contract with Gladys Mosier and Claude Thornhill
382.s: They drew up a contract as personal representatives with 25 percent each; little came of it at first, and Kirby managed himself.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: When I met Gladys and Claude that day, we had a contract already drawn up which I signed, in fact Jenny and I both signed the contract,

382.t: How the Carter tour came about and the Decca switch
382.s: She was contacted under her management contract; unsure if it coincided with signing at Decca.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Well I was contacted, and as I said before, by this time I was under management of MCA, and this was their first experience with singers, I suppose. They were more band oriented.

382.t: Who guided her career after Claude: Lou Singer, Columbia and MCA
382.s: After the break with Claude, Lou Singer arranged for her; Columbia's artists bureau ended and she moved to MCA.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: Well after I sort of broke off with Claude and he was no longer working with me I got you know, I sort of got hung up with that folk song bag and I had to keep looking around for material. So I

382.t: Claude's artistic control, her name change and early publicity
382.s: Claude's role was artistic, he picked the name Sullivan, and she tells how Archer Winston's article came about.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: When I came to New York I had been using the name Maxine Williams at the B.H.L. Club. But I think I mentioned previously that, well there was a singer making recordings and was on the air by the name of Midge Williams and I guess he supposed there would be some sort of a conflict, and it was his…

509.t: Joel Seigel as friend and not-quite manager
509.s: She says Joel Seigel was a witty friend who never really managed her and failed to book a contract or flights.
509.q: Oh, child, Joel was my friend. I thought he was my friend. But Joel got carried away with . . . I think it happened to him in Hollywood. We went to the City Grill and all

509.s: She asked Verve's Sheila Mathis to manage her; Sheila straightened out the business; John Levy's quiet help.
509.q: She said, ―Okay.‖ She took all the business, changed some stuff. She straightened everything out. I‘m not getting Joel Seigel. [laughs] I had to laugh after it was all over. ―Well, I didn‘t know I was supposed to do all that.‖ ―What you going to do? You‘re going to type up a contract and make my…

509.t: John Levy as her manager since she was eighteen
509.s: She says she still works with John Levy by handshake, with no contract, since about eighteen.
509.q: I‘m still with John Levy. We never had a contract. We shook hands; I guess I was eighteen. I was eighteen, yes. And I said, ―Are you going to be my manager?‖ Ai, yi, yi. But, you know, he had all the big people. He had the big acts. He tried. He tried. He tried hard. But when I said I‘m going to…

509.t: John Levy and his roster of top acts
509.s: She explains John Levy managed Wes Montgomery, Nancy Wilson, Joe Williams and Cannonball and cared for her.
509.ch: Staying home, image and being a woman leader
509.q: That‘s right. At that time, John Levy had, oh, good lord, he had all the top acts. He had Wes Montgomery. Well, he‘s had Nancy Wilson and Joe Williams for fifty years.

473.t: Cab advises loyalty to Sammy Burke, who confronts Glaser
473.s: Cab told him to stick with the man who brought him this far; when Jones confessed, Burke stormed into Glaser's office threatening his license and the job was arranged.
473.ch: Fred Astaire and the high points
473.q: He said, "It's very easy." He said, "Stick with the same man that brought you as far as you have come." And he says, "If Fred Astaire wants you, he's going to get you. That man is no fool. He's been in this business for years. He wants you and Joe can't deliver you, --"

473.t: Sammy Burke proposes a small group and Ben Bart turns him down
473.s: Recording around Broadway for small labels, he met agent Sammy Burke, who advised forming a quartet; Universal's Ben Bart refused him as too experienced, so Burke quit his job to manage him personally.
473.ch: Return to New York and the Embers
473.q: So in the meantime, I had this paper and looking at it, and so, fooling around down Broadway, you know, as usual, walking around seeing the different guys, you know, making a little record here and there. I forget the guy we made the records with. We were making a lot of stuff with Coleman Hawkins…

473.t: Cruise with Cab and the dilemma of asking Cab instead of Sammy
473.s: On a nostalgia cruise with Cab and his wife they reminisced; Jones explains he could not ask Sammy about Glaser's offer, since Sammy might have exploded, and Dance says Sam knew what he was doing.
473.q: last year, and by celebrating it we went on the cruise he was on, you know, a nostalgia cruise. And as I told you, Tedd King, Hildegarde, Peter Duchin and Cab and his daughter.

473.t: Sam Burke's faith in him, starting at forty-five
473.s: His career really started at 45; Jones credits his manager Sam Burke, who believed in a nearly finished trumpeter and told him he could not make people buy the records alone.
473.q: When I first come out of the Sunday school band, I first left, I said when I'm 40 years old I'm coming out of it. I thought that was old. Then I didn't get started till I was 45. I didn't get started till I was 45. But the great thing about it, let me say this about Sam Burke, that is the man. He…

226.t: Becoming manager; Ed Fuerst as road manager; setting up offices
226.s: Ed Fuerst became Shearing's road manager, Levy the manager, and they opened offices in New York as John Levy Enterprises.
226.ch: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
226.q: I got off the road [to perform as manager]. We got to have another road manager, so he hired Ed [Fuerst] – he hired a friend of his [George’s]. . .

226.t: Looking beyond bass and becoming Shearing's adviser
226.s: He saw himself in the business end and started advising Shearing, who valued his trustworthiness, as did Leonard Feather.
226.ch: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
226.q: It’s like your roots, how you start out, what – if you are in communication with and you are working side-by-side with people like that, it’s bound to develop you into – to get the very best out of you. Also, your stature – you came along with these people and you rose with these people, so their…

226.t: Why he moved from playing bass to road managing
226.s: Shearing's wife was inexperienced as road manager, so Levy realized he could not both play bass and handle the business.
226.ch: From bassist to George Shearing's road manager
226.q: I realized that – after we made that first trip out and we were doing a lot of dates where we were working with a guarantee and a percentage – that – and I was acting as [the road manager] – Shearing’s wife was the road manager, considered the road manager, road person, but she had no experience at…

123.t: Wayne's path into the business and booking together
123.s: Wayne went from disco to working with him at the North Park, Rush Street and the Blackstone, and now they book together.
123.q: No, he was into disco and all that stuff, and I got him working with me when he was about twenty - I guess he started. And he worked with me at the North Park and he

123.t: Financing the club and Wayne as the main man
123.s: He leaves the loan negotiations to Wayne, who took over around the Grand Avenue years.
123.q: I don’t know, Wayne handled that, so I don’t know. He’s the main man now.

123.t: Wayne takes over the business side; hotels and four-night runs
123.s: He says Wayne handles licenses and money, and explains the cost of rooms and why multi-night runs beat one-nighters.
123.ch: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
123.q: No at the North Park we didn’t handle it at all, we had nothing to do with it. And in fact, they handled all the licensing and they also gave us rooms for the traveling musicians at the hotels, which was great. Now we’ve got all that expense on us.

758.t: Sam Beers, Joe Glaser and hard times
758.s: His manager Sam Beers blocked a California offer and sold his contract to Joe Glaser; Roy pawned a ring to move the band.
758.q: : In the meantime, I got an offer to go out to California with Bing Crosby's brother. And everything was going along great, except the guy didn't want me to leave, you know, because we was doin' business for him. So he stopped it. How he stopped it I'm not too sure yet, but he did.

758.t: Return to the Savoy and meeting Joe Glaser
758.s: At the Savoy Roy hosted young trumpeters, and Glaser demanded he come to his office or not work.
758.ch: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
758.q: : And I came to the Savoy, and all the cats used to come up there and sit in -- Dizzy, Joe Guy, Charlie, Bobby Moore, all the little trumpet players that was around in those days. And they know my records better than I did. They all knew the solos, I mean. So they would sit in.

758.t: Buying out his Glaser contract to join Krupa
758.s: Glaser let Frank Vernier buy his contract for a thousand dollars after Charlie Barnet balked.
758.q: : So things kind of petered out in Chicago, and I went to New York to see Glaser... Because I had an apartment there, on Michigan Boulevard...not Michigan, on 55th -- 55th and Michigan. When I went back to New York, then I got Waverly(?) to come back with me... No, I went to see Glaser. I called…

452.t: Ben Barth stood by him; why he carries heavy insurance
452.s: Cobb says Ben Barth stayed in his corner and he never borrowed from him, helped by insurance that he still carries heavily.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: I stayed with Ben all the way. Ben was in my corner all the way. He didn't know if I was going to come back, but he still stuck with me and still sold the told (inaudible), I got money over here. If you ever need anything. -- I never got in debt. I never borrowed $100.00 from him. I took care of…

452.t: MCA exploits Herbie Fields until Joe Glazer places him with Hampton
452.s: Cobb relates how MCA bled Fields's family out of $80,000 for air time and passed him over for another act until Joe Glazer rescued him and put him with Hampton at $250 a week.
452.q: So they put him in New Jersey at the Meadowbrook -- what is it? Daly, Frank Daly? Meadowbrook, and they had Herbert playing for air time. They bled Herbert and his mother's husband, who's a jeweler in Newark, New Jersey, out of $80,000.00. But they were doing all this. And Herbert, see, what was…

452.t: Ben Barth's death and how Cobb brought James Brown to Universal
452.s: Cobb says Ben Barth died in 1966, and that Barth signed James Brown after Cobb screened him in Macon, Georgia.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: Yeah. See, Ben didn't die until I come back to Houston. He died in 1966. I come back to Houston in '59. Ben dropped dead on the golf course in Miami, and Jack, his son, was walking with him when he died. See, they had a boat house down there in Miami, and Maxine and he lived -- spent a lot of time…

83.t: Managing Jimmy Clanton and sending him to a choreographer
83.s: Matassa managed Clanton for three years; he found him hard to manage and could not get him to learn a nightclub act or stage presence.
83.q: and he wouldn't do it I had a medley of his hits done the kind of thing you open up with or close with that kind of thing you never would learn that

83.s: Matassa recorded and managed the Spiders, switching them from gospel to R&B, buying uniforms and a station wagon and sending Phyllis Boone on the road, without seeking profit.
83.q: A couple of times I recorded people, but I recorded them because I thought they needed to be recorded. I mean, you know, like the Spiders, for instance.

911.s: Rowe notes even stars like Clark Terry asked for gigs; Brown says that is true in this genre.

911.t: Solo versus groups, Jeff Coffin duo, and emailing European festivals
911.s: Why he often works alone, recent Jeff Coffin duo and big band albums, and the mass emailing of 1,200 festivals that won six European gigs.
911.q: Yeah. It’s funny. I’m kind of coming around to the other side where my last two albums have now — the last one I just had was February 26 with Jeff Coffin, a duo, and it’s just the two of us playing saxophone. And then the one before that I wrote a big band album and it’s kind of my sound, it’s…

640.s: She discusses animosity directed at her and why agents are in an untenable position and bend the truth.
640.q: I ran into a lot of animosity, I should say that, because people are jealous and deeply threatened and particularly because Bob is a Piscean and he’s a very gentle man, and people couldn’t understand why he was suddenly getting so taciturn and hard-nosed you know. And a lot of the time it was his…

640.s: She took on promoting Bob's career, writing NEA grants, driven by tenacity and her northern English upbringing.

So now, you know, when you’re first writing music, I mean you dream of having a career and people asking you…

680.t: Saving the Belfast concerts and Wein's help launching Burton's band

680.s: The Toronto weeks gel, the stay becomes three years, and Burton acts as band manager, learning the promoters who later book his own band.

By the end of the two weeks, the group had kind of jelled into a sound and a comfort level. So he said, “I got some more concerts coming up in the next few weeks;…

426.t: Assigning days of the week to Blue Note, Prestige, Savoy and Vox
426.s: He chose to stay solo and sold fixed weekdays to each company, which paid whether they used them or not.
426.q: Right. Now that’s interesting because that brought on…necessity is the mother of invention. The only way I could solve that dilemma. When there were more people wanting more time and I was only one person. Also that was a point of decision for me to get bigger or stay small. I could have hired some…

426.ch: Later career, remasters and other interests
426.q: Yeah, that’s a big company. C.T.I was a small company with a lot of money but when it got to be Verve, that’s a big company. I used to—its peculiar that they…When I got a date for one of these big companies, they’d sent me a purchase order for the studio time. Can you imagine what they asked me to…

230.t: Six months as Carlos Gastell's partner managing singers
230.s: After breaking up the 1949 band he spent about six months at Gastell's management firm, whose clients included Peggy Lee, Mel Torme and Nat Cole, and found it boring.
230.ch: The 1949 band, breakup and later years
230.q: Oh, maybe six months. It's hard to -- I found it very boring, very boring and irritating, and Carlos was a one man operation. Carlos never needed a partner of any kind. I mean he was a dynamo of a man, I mean in handling

But I wanted out of the music business for awhile, but I went with him and I stayed with him about six months, six, seven months, just for something to do, to see if I'd like it. I didn't like it. Because you…

409.t: Agencies and the fifty percent cut
409.s: Booking agencies demanded fifty percent of the band; he refused at first with the William Morris Agency but then went with Moe Gale.
409.q: So I said, 'Well, I ain't going to give up no part of my band.' And it squares me out. So that's the time I came in with Moe Gale.

409.s: Cherry Red Blues and Things Ain't What They Used to Be made him successful; he stopped paying fifty percent and bookings dropped.
409.q: I had "Cherry Red Blues", yeah. And "Things Ain't What They Used to Be". And they didn't squeeze me out. I got in all the major theaters cross country. And I played everything.

18.s: He says agents got you money and he never met double contracts.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: They would try to get you money and whatever they would get, they would give it to you. They would see that you get it.

18.t: Musicians' views of John Hammond and Joe Glaser
18.s: Nobody said anything bad of Hammond; Glaser was disliked but would bawl you out if you asked for much.
18.q: Well, he was going to bawl you out if you asked for a lot of money...

74.t: Sparks as road manager; the band books itself
74.s: Sparks becomes road manager; the band has no other manager and books itself.

74.q: I don't know of any other.

149.s: He signed with Gale after a year or two at the Savoy, valuing a home base.

124.t: Joe Loco leaves for Arnold Shaw's agency
124.s: After McRae built him up with three dates a night, Loco jumped to a new agent, and radio disc jockeys dropped his records.
124.q: We wouldn't take any (inaudible). We'd take like four hundred and fifty dollars and do two hours, (Inaudible) so and so at 168th Street.

77.s: She mostly booked herself, suspecting agents of knocking down, and one theater job led to another.
77.q: Most of the time I did it myself. But sometimes some agent would ask me if I would -- but I didn't bother much with the agents. 103.t: Willard Alexander, Milt Ebbins and Joe Glasser

241.t: No manager and no booking book

773.t: Octave Boye, Billy Marrero and her husband as band manager

562.t: Booking herself after leaving an agency

998.q: Holly. Holly has been really good about that. And I’ve been one that I’ve always been pretty self-sufficient. 341.s: Maricle books DIVA, Five Play and the 3-D Jazz Trio herself, often eight hours a day; the shutdown let her practise for hours and love the drums again, with Jami Dauber managing.

583.t: John Levy and working for free

975.s: His cell phone is his manager; he has steady work without fame.
975.q: My manager is the cell phone in my pocket which I hope I turned off. But yeah, people call and I have enough work to keep me happy. 983.t: The Catch-22 of turning down calls to work with his own band
983.s: Rowe asks whether he must refuse other work; Williams explains the dilemma of bookings and wanting to keep doing other things.
983.q: Well it’s a Catch 22 situation. I’m like, “This is a stupid conversation.” Like I said when I said I was in the…

400.t: Eddie South's mother on his paper route and manager Sam Scholnick
400.s: Hinton collects the paper money from Eddie South's mother, sees his European photos, and hears of a manager trying to bring the "Dark Angel of Violin" back to a Chicago hotel.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: Boy, she was beautiful. SPEKAER: Well in terms of… you were talking about your newspaper route and some of the other things that you were doing. Now you met Eddie South, at least his mother, when you were doing this.

114.t: Promoters see dollar signs; Stan Getz's light schedule
114.s: Promoters ignore the toll, whereas Stan Getz had days off between gigs; he links this to Dizzy.
114.ch: Practice, the road and Dizzy's death
114.q: They -- but it would be nice if like -- Stan Getz had the thing going for him, man, like, he would go play one gig, then he'd have two days off. He'd play another gig, there'd be 3 days off. And the guy would still be getting paid. That was nice.

672.t: Family before business; her husband briefly managing her
672.s: She explains John Levy always knew her life came first, and that her husband and lawyer took over management briefly.
672.q: Oh yeah. That happened long before. That was in the first conversation I had with John Levy. John knew all along that whatever my life is going to be, my life comes first, and he was just like my dad. He was very much like my father. Not like him, but he was a father to me. So I knew that he knew…

373.t: The power of a Down Beat review: Charlie Ventura
373.s: He realized the economic power of his reviews when Ventura's manager complained.
373.ch: Black writers, Harvard and Down Beat
373.q: Oh yeah. I used to – I had to review it, because it came in, but I never understood Charlie Ventura. I thought it was mainly playing notes at a hard tempo, and loud. One day his manager called me up and said, “What have you got personally against Charlie? You’re really hurting him economically.” I…

408.t: Down Beat polls, Charles Ives and guest-list policy
408.s: Awards, 'Prizes are for children', and not giving freebies.
408.q: Well, yeah, you know it’s just a policy.

109.t: Milt Shaw's threat at Gothenburg; Lorraine becomes Dizzy's manager
109.s: Billy Shaw's son threatened him on the tender into Gothenburg; Clarke urged Lorraine to manage Dizzy herself, and she has done so ever since.
109.q: So after all this came up, all these things, so we arrived in Sweden, and his father made him come back. He was supposed to travel with us. All this 20,000, or $27,000.00, I forget exactly how much money, but I know it was a large sum of money, he was supposed to travel with the band and all. So…

80.s: Autrey hesitantly calls Kirkeby a capable business man who almost owned Victor but was not on Autrey's personal side.
80.q: there to -- smooth operator. He was working for Victor. Victor had to let him go. He almost owned Victor.

377.t: Road manager coming out of Kansas City
377.s: Basie says Snodgrass was not his first road manager; a man who decided himself to be the manager came out of Kansas City with him.
377.ch: Carnegie Hall, nicknames and later career

113.t: GAC books 40 one-nighters and McShann pays off Gale
113.s: Berle Adams at GAC booked 40 one-nighters; McShann paid off Gale with a check in Cincinnati to Ben Bart, who had expected to take over.
113.ch: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
113.q: I say, yeah, but you just got through explaining to me, though, that this is not a loan office, so -- he says, well, it is not but we expect to get our money eventually, so anyway I got a call from Tomino so Tomino told me, he says, don't make no move, don't care what they tell you, just take it…

614.s: Dressel took over as manager in 1968; he had run a music store and worked in record promotion, was a drummer in early rock and roll groups, and had been a fan since his teens.
614.q: Well, he'd done many things. I think the -- well, he was already into working as a promotion man for the people that handle artists and so on. And prior to that, he once owned a music store in Connecticut.

26.s: Mills managed from the Kentucky Club and traveled with them first class.
26.q: At the Kentucky Club. He become our official manager when in fact, he managed us when we went from the Kentucky Club too, to Cotton Club. He handled a lot of recordings for Duke's songs, because he never managed no band. But he had a big publishing house at 49th and Broadway in the Brill Building.…

87.s: Glaser started as Granz's secretary, scaled theaters sharply, and later managed Erroll Garner.
87.q: Uh-huh. Later on. And he really got -- he really got that thing going big in Europe though when he finally started it, you know. He got a big deal going in Europe. But he had a girl helping him who was a tremendous help, I thought. That was Martha Glaser.

378.t: Booker Max Cavelli and Joe Glaser's honesty
378.s: Norvo praises booker Max Cavelli as steady and honest, like Joe Glaser, who always gave a straight answer.
378.ch: Las Vegas, Sinatra and later years
378.q: But Max is steady as a jazz booker and I think the guys respect him for that. When jazz wasn't doing so well, a few years back, he still tried to keep fellas like Charlie Shavers and Roy Eldridge, everybody, tried to keep them working --

166.t: Years with Garner and Martha Glaser's role in his exit
166.s: He was with Garner from late 1949 to 1952; manager Martha Glaser wanted him gone.
166.ch: Erroll Garner, the 1952 arrest and Florida
166.q: Well, as soon as he came back from Paris, I was from Erroll from '49, the latter part of '49 -- I think it was the latter part of '49. In fact, I'm almost sure it was the latter part of '49. Then '49, '50, '51, '52. And then I got arrested, and he was told not to come near me. It would do something…

379.s: He refuses terms of booking offices and demands contracts.
379.ch: The Latin scene and business of the 1940s-70s
379.q: What it did for the band, it would always happen, for some reason at all. This is a _______ country. Too many things (unintelligible) here. And always a (unintelligible). Yeah, but, yeah, but. So we got lots of the jobs. Then everybody said, well, (unintelligible).

120.t: Withholding taxes, the Salt City Six and a different band in Toronto each time
120.s: Ann had to figure each sideman's withholding, so in 1971 he joined the Salt City Six; in Toronto he never had the same band twice.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: Well, almost like there is today - like I'm doing today; I'm here - I am in Detroit, Michigan -- I'm working with a band by myself with an organized band and that has proven, in the last few years, to me, that that's the way to go for me because - at that time - it was a terrible job for my wife to…

233.t: John Levy's plan, taxes, and the sidemen's status
233.s: Manager John Levy said Wes had outgrown clubs; Monk and Buddy were sidemen in business terms, which caused some distance.
233.ch: Wes's death and Monk's turning point
233.q: And I remember very distinctly we were working a concert; and we weren't working, we were beginning to lean on...Well, as a matter of fact, John Levy, his personal manager, had come out to California, I believe it was. His manager and the publicity man, they had a meeting saying 'Wes had outgrown…

234.t: Revenge is costly; the music marketplace; Capitol money withheld
234.s: Gil says revenge is too costly and describes waiting on money from Capitol held by a lawyer.
234.q: In a way it's a waste of time to, what do you call it, to overbeat it, you know what I mean. Like once the horse is dead there is no use beating it. So a lot of it, while still alive and you can make people squirm and move over for you and give you some opportunity, it works fine. When it becomes…

95.t: Mr. Pierce, the withheld mail and the missing years
95.s: Her manager Mr. Pierce kept her mail so she did not know the record companies wanted her; she was living with her brother in Chicago.
95.q: No, after -- see, around then, Mr. told me that Mr. Pierce wasn't up there no more. But he carried me over -- I got this contract from the Victor people, but my brother wouldn't let me (unintelligible).

76.t: Taking Slim Gaillard's money seriously: William Morris and the box office
76.s: Zutty insisted on being paid by theater management through the William Morris office because Slim Gaillard was known to take money; Slim lost his house at auction for unpaid taxes.
76.q: But Zutty had, he went on that tour with them through the William Morris office. He had them to take care of the business. Because Slim Gaillard was known to be a character that would take your money. And he was so surprised the first week they got paid, they paid Zutty directly from the box…

238.s: She and Willard recall Gastel's loud shirts and warmth and how he got her recognition and good pay.
238.ch: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
238.q: Everybody loved him, because he loved everybody. He loved people, you know, he was just that type of person. And -- well, I really considered myself lucky to be handled by somebody like him, you know.

239.t: John Levy as mentor, business manager and friend
239.s: Levy's business sense, closeness to Jones's family, and their handshake management arrangement.
239.ch: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
239.q: And well, of course, he was close to my family, like my father and my aunts and my uncles and all that. So he feels like a -- still feels like a big brother, you know? And I think we destroyed the theory that friendship and business doesn't work, because we've been doing business and we're still…

112.s: After Lyons went home, Wooding managed the band himself until returning to America.
112.q: : So I managed myself clean until I came back to America.
